reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases; CDC parasitic disease guidance
clinicalPearls: The leading infective cause of eosinophilic meningitis worldwide, caused by the rat lungworm Angiostrongylus cantonensis
Acquired by eating raw or undercooked snails and slugs, or paratenic hosts such as freshwater prawns, crabs and frogs, or contaminated unwashed produce
Endemic in Southeast Asia and the Pacific, with expanding distribution including parts of the Americas
Presents with severe headache, neck stiffness, nausea and often striking paraesthesiae or hyperaesthesia; cranial nerve palsies can occur
Cerebrospinal fluid characteristically shows a raised opening pressure with eosinophilic pleocytosis
A related species, Angiostrongylus costaricensis, instead causes abdominal (intestinal) angiostrongyliasis

Management is largely supportive, with analgesia, repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture to relieve pressure and headache, and corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction; the role of anthelmintics is debated
Most immunocompetent patients recover, but heavy infections can cause lasting neurological damage or death
reference.pathophysiology: Angiostrongylus cantonensis completes its natural cycle in rats and molluscs. Humans become accidental hosts by ingesting third-stage larvae in raw or undercooked snails, slugs or paratenic hosts, or on contaminated produce. The larvae penetrate the intestine, enter the circulation and migrate to the central nervous system, where they cannot complete development. Their migration and death within the brain, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid provoke an intense eosinophil-rich inflammatory response, producing eosinophilic meningitis with raised intracranial pressure. Dying larvae and the surrounding inflammation account for the headache, sensory disturbances and, in severe cases, focal neurological injury.
additionalDifferentials: Gnathostomiasis and other parasitic causes of eosinophilic meningitis
Central nervous system malignancy or drug-induced eosinophilic meningitis
additionalInvestigations: Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid cell count and differential
Cerebrospinal fluid and blood eosinophil quantification
Serology or molecular testing for Angiostrongylus where available
MRI of the brain for migratory or inflammatory lesions
Dietary and exposure history (snails, slugs, prawns, unwashed vegetables)
Exclusion of tuberculous, fungal and neoplastic causes of eosinophilic meningitis
redFlags: Depressed consciousness or focal neurological deficit
Cranial nerve palsies or visual involvement
Signs of severe or complicated meningoencephalitis
reference.prognosis: Most immunocompetent patients recover over weeks with supportive care, though headache and paraesthesiae may be prolonged; heavy larval burdens can cause permanent neurological sequelae or death.
pitfalls: Not requesting a cerebrospinal fluid differential and thereby missing the eosinophilic pleocytosis
Overlooking the exposure history to snails, slugs or unwashed produce
Giving anthelmintics without corticosteroid cover, which may worsen inflammation as larvae die
Failing to relieve raised intracranial pressure with therapeutic lumbar puncture
Confusing it with the abdominal disease caused by Angiostrongylus costaricensis
management: Corticosteroids to suppress the eosinophilic inflammatory response and shorten the headache and neurological symptoms
Serial therapeutic lumbar punctures to relieve raised intracranial pressure and headache
Analgesia and supportive care for headache and paraesthesiae during the largely self-limiting course
Anthelmintic therapy such as albendazole only with concurrent corticosteroid cover and by specialist decision, as killing larvae can intensify inflammation
Neurological monitoring for complications such as cranial nerve palsies and focal deficits, with escalation for severe intracranial hypertension
Preventive advice on thoroughly cooking snails, slugs and freshwater crustaceans and washing produce
